Good is Jehovah, my Lord, a Levite sent out by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people of Judah in the law ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).

Pleasing to Jehovah, the “servant,” the “Ammonite,” who joined with those who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the Exile ([Neh. 2:10](#Neh.2.10)). He was a man of great influence, which he exerted in opposition to the Jews, and “sent letters” to Nehemiah “to put him in fear” ([Neh. 6:17-19](#Neh.6.17)). “Eliashib the priest” prepared for him during Nehemiah’s absence “a chamber in the courts of the house of God,” which on his return grieved Nehemiah sore, and therefore he “cast forth all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the chamber” (13:7, 8).
Id., a Levite sent out through Judah by Jehoshaphat to teach the people ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).
A son of Gomer, and grandson of Japheth ([Gen. 10:3](#Gen.10.3)).

A king of Hamath, who sent “Joram his son unto King David to salute him,” when he “heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer” ([2 Sam. 8:9](#2Sam.8.9), [10](#2Sam.8.10)). Called Tou ([1 Chr. 18:9](#1Chr.18.9), [10](#1Chr.18.10)).
A judge of the tribe of Issachar who “judged” Israel twenty-three years ([Judg. 10:1](#Judg.10.1), [2](#Judg.10.2)), when he died, and was buried in Shamir. He was succeeded by Jair.

A foster-child, an Ephesian who accompanied Paul during a part of his third missionary journey ([Acts 20:4](#Acts.20.4); [21:29](#Acts.21.29)). He was with Paul in Jerusalem, and the Jews, supposing that the apostle had brought him with him into the temple, raised a tumult which resulted in Paul’s imprisonment. (See  TEMPLE, HEROD’S.) In writing to Timothy, the apostle says, “Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick” ([2 Tim. 4:20](#2Tim.4.20)). This must refer to some event not noticed in the Acts.
The son of Lamech and Zillah, “an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron” ([Gen. 4:22](#Gen.4.22); R.V., “the forger of every cutting instrument of brass and iron”).

Chance, an Asiatic Christian, a “faithful minister in the Lord” ([Eph. 6:21](#Eph.6.21), [22](#Eph.6.22)), who, with Trophimus, accompanied Paul on a part of his journey from Macedonia to Jerusalem ([Acts 20:4](#Acts.20.4)). He is alluded to also in [Col. 4:7](#Col.4.7), [Titus 3:12](#Titus.3.12), and [2 Tim. 4:12](#2Tim.4.12) as having been with Paul at Rome, whence he sent him to Ephesus, probably for the purpose of building up and encouraging the church there.

Prince, a Greek rhetorician, in whose “school” at Ephesus Paul disputed daily for the space of two years with those who came to him ([Acts 19:9](#Acts.19.9)). Some have supposed that he was a Jew, and that his “school” was a private synagogue.
The name of a person to whom Agur’s words are addressed ([Prov. 30:1](#Prov.30.1)).
A Levite whom David appointed to take part in bringing the ark up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom by playing the psaltery on that occasion ([1 Chr. 15:18](#1Chr.15.18), [20](#1Chr.15.20)).
A Levite who returned with Zerubbabel from the Captivity ([Neh. 12:9](#Neh.12.9)).

A Hittite, the husband of Bathsheba, whom David first seduced, and then after Uriah’s death married. He was one of the band of David’s “mighty men.” The sad story of the curel wrongs inflicted upon him by David and of his mournful death are simply told in the sacred record ([2 Sam. 11:2-12:26](#2Sam.11.2)).
A Kohathite ancestor of the prophet Samuel ([1 Chr. 6:36](#1Chr.6.36)).
The chief of the Kohathites at the time when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 15:5](#1Chr.15.5), [11](#1Chr.15.11)).
The father of Michaiah, one of Rehoboam’s wives, and mother of Abijah ([2 Chr. 13:2](#2Chr.13.2)).

A high priest in the time of Ahaz ([2 Kings 16:10-16](#2Kgs.16.10)), at whose bidding he constructed an idolatrous altar like one the king had seen at Damascus, to be set up instead of the brazen altar.
The father of Meremoth, mentioned in [Ezra 8:33](#Ezra.8.33).

A prophet of Kirjath-jearim in the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah ([Jer. 26:20-23](#Jer.26.20)). He fled into Egypt from the cruelty of the king, but having been brought back he was beheaded and his body “cast into the graves of the common people.”
One of the priests who stood at the right hand of Ezra’s pulpit when he read and expounded the law ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
The son of Aram, and grandson of Shem ([Gen. 10:23](#Gen.10.23); [1 Chr. 1:17](#1Chr.1.17)).
One of the Horite “dukes” in the land of Edom ([Gen. 36:28](#Gen.36.28)).

A wanderer, a descendant of Joktan ([Gen. 10:27](#Gen.10.27); [1 Chr. 1:21](#1Chr.1.21)), the founder apparently of one of the Arab tribes; the name also probably of the province they occupied and of their chief city.

Strength, a son of Abinadab, in whose house the men of Kirjath-jearim placed the ark when it was brought back from the land of the Philistines ([1 Sam. 7:1](#1Sam.7.1)). He with his brother Ahio drove the cart on which the ark was placed when David sought to bring it up to Jerusalem. When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah, in direct violation of the divine law ([Num. 4:15](#Num.4.15)), put forth his hand to steady the ark, and was immediately smitten unto death. The place where this occurred was henceforth called Perez-uzzah ([1 Chr. 13:11](#1Chr.13.11)). David on this feared to proceed further, and placed the ark in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite ([2 Sam. 6:2-11](#2Sam.6.2); [1 Chr. 13:6-13](#1Chr.13.6)).
The son of Bukki, and a descendant of Aaron ([1 Chr. 6:5](#1Chr.6.5), [51](#1Chr.6.51); [Ezra 7:4](#Ezra.7.4)).
A son of Bela, and grandson of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 7:7](#1Chr.7.7)).
A Benjamite, a chief in the tribe ([1 Chr. 9:8](#1Chr.9.8)).
A son of Bani. He had the oversight of the Levites after the return from captivity ([Neh. 11:22](#Neh.11.22)).
The head of the house of Jedaiah, one of “the chief of the priests” ([Neh. 12:19](#Neh.12.19)).
A priest who assisted in the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem ([Neh. 12:42](#Neh.12.42)).

One of Amaziah’s sons, whom the people made king of Judah in his father’s stead ([2 Kings 14:21](#2Kgs.14.21); [2 Chr. 26:1](#2Chr.26.1)). His long reign of about fifty-two years was “the most prosperous excepting that of Jehosaphat since the time of Solomon.” He was a vigorous and able ruler, and “his name spread abroad, even to the entering in of Egypt” ([2 Chr. 26:8](#2Chr.26.8), [14](#2Chr.26.14)). In the earlier part of his reign, under the influence of Zechariah, he was faithful to Jehovah, and “did that which was right in the sight of the Lord” ([2 Kings 15:3](#2Kgs.15.3); [2 Chr. 26:4](#2Chr.26.4), [5](#2Chr.26.5)); but toward the close of his long life “his heart was lifted up to his destruction,” and he wantonly invaded the priest’s office ([2 Chr. 26:16](#2Chr.26.16)), and entering the sanctuary proceeded to offer incense on the golden altar. Azariah the high priest saw the tendency of such a daring act on the part of the king, and with a band of eighty priests he withstood him ([2 Chr. 26:17](#2Chr.26.17)), saying, “It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense.” Uzziah was suddenly struck with leprosy while in the act of offering incense (26:19-21), and he was driven from the temple and compelled to reside in “a several house” to the day of his death ([2 Kings 15:5](#2Kgs.15.5), [27](#2Kgs.15.27); [2 Chr. 26:3](#2Chr.26.3)). He was buried in a separate grave “in the field of the burial which belonged to the kings” ([2 Kings 15:7](#2Kgs.15.7); [2 Chr. 26:23](#2Chr.26.23)). “That lonely grave in the royal necropolis would eloquently testify to coming generations that all earthly monarchy must bow before the inviolable order of the divine will, and that no interference could be tolerated with that unfolding of the purposes of God, which, in the fulness of time, would reveal the Christ, the true High Priest and King for evermore” (Dr. Green’s Kingdom of Israel, etc.).
The father of Jehonathan, one of David’s overseers ([1 Chr. 27:25](#1Chr.27.25)).
One of the sons of Kohath, and uncle of Aaron ([Ex. 6:18](#Exod.6.18); [Lev. 10:4](#Lev.10.4)).
One of the sons of Heman ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4)); called also Azareel (18).
A son of Bela, and grandson of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 7:7](#1Chr.7.7)).
Purity; worthy of honour, one of Haman’s sons, whom the Jews slew in the palace of Shushan ([Esther 9:9](#Esth.9.9)).

Beautiful, the queen of Ahasuerus, who was deposed from her royal dignity because she refused to obey the king when he desired her to appear in the banqueting hall of Shushan the palace ([Esther 1:10-12](#Esth.1.10)).
The son of Shemath. He conspired against Joash, king of Judah, and slew him ([2 Chr. 24:25](#2Chr.24.25), [26](#2Chr.24.26)). He is called also Jozachar ([2 Kings 12:21](#2Kgs.12.21)).
One of David’s valiant men ([1 Chr. 11:41](#1Chr.11.41)), the descendant of Ahlai, of the “children of Sheshan” (2:31).
The father of Baruch, who “earnestly repaired” part of the wall of Jerusalem ([Neh. 3:20](#Neh.3.20); marg., “Zaccai”).
An ancestor of Achan ([Josh. 7:1](#Josh.7.1), [17](#Josh.7.17), [18](#Josh.7.18)). He is probably the “Zimri” of [1 Chr. 2:6](#1Chr.2.6).
Called “the Shiphmite,” one of David’s officers, who had charge of his vineyards ([1 Chr. 27:27](#1Chr.27.27)).
The father of Jashobeam, who was one of David’s officers ([1 Chr. 27:2](#1Chr.27.2)).
An overseer of the priests after the Captivity ([Neh. 11:14](#Neh.11.14)).
Gift, the son of Nathan, who was “king’s friend” in the court of Solomon ([1 Kings 4:5](#1Kgs.4.5)).
Pure, one whose “sons” returned with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem ([Ezra 2:9](#Ezra.2.9); [Neh. 7:14](#Neh.7.14)).

Pure, a superintendant of customs; a chief tax-gather (publicanus) at Jericho ([Luke 19:1-10](#Luke.19.1)). “The collection of customs at Jericho, which at this time produced and exported a considerable quantity of balsam, was undoubtedly an important post, and would account for Zacchaeus being a rich man.” Being short of stature, he hastened on before the multitude who were thronging about Christ as he passed through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, and climbed up a sycamore tree that he might be able to see him. When our Lord reached the spot he looked up to the publican among the branches, and addressing him by name, told him to make haste and come down, as he intended that day to abide at his house. This led to the remarkable interview recorded by the evangelist, and to the striking parable of the ten pounds ([Luke 19:12-27](#Luke.19.12)). At Er-riha (Jericho) there is a large, venerable looking square tower, which goes by the traditional name of the House of Zacchaeus.
A son of Asaph, and chief of one of the courses of singers as arranged by David ([1 Chr. 25:2](#1Chr.25.2), [10](#1Chr.25.10)).
Father of Shammua, who was one of the spies sent out by Moses ([Num. 13:4](#Num.13.4)).

Son of Jeroboam II., king of Israel. On the death of his father there was an interregnum of ten years, at the end of which he succeeded to the throne, which he occupied only six months, having been put to death by Shallum, who usurped the throne. “He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his fathers had done” ([2 Kings 14:29](#2Kgs.14.29); [15:8-12](#2Kgs.15.8)). In him the dynasty of Jehu came to an end.

A priest of the course of Abia, the eighth of the twenty-four courses into which the priests had been originally divided by David ([1 Chr. 23:1-19](#1Chr.23.1)). Only four of these courses or “families” of the priests returned from the Exile ([Ezra 2:36-39](#Ezra.2.36)); but they were then re-distributed under the old designations. The priests served at the temple twice each year, and only for a week each time. Zacharias’s time had come for this service. During this period his home would be one of the chambers set apart for the priests on the sides of the temple ground. …

The son or grandson of Jehoiada, the high priest in the times of Ahaziah and Joash. After the death of Jehoiada he boldly condemned both the king and the people for their rebellion against God ([2 Chr. 24:20](#2Chr.24.20)), which so stirred up their resentment against him that at the king’s commandment they stoned him with stones, and he died “in the court of the house of the Lord” (24:21). Christ alludes to this deed of murder in [Matt. 23:35](#Matt.23.35), [Luke 11:51](#Luke.11.51).
Memorial, a son of Jehiel ([1 Chr. 8:31](#1Chr.8.31); [9:35](#1Chr.9.35)); called Zechariah (9:37).

A son of Ahitub, of the line of Eleazer ([2 Sam. 8:17](#2Sam.8.17); [1 Chr. 24:3](#1Chr.24.3)), high priest in the time of David ([2 Sam. 20:25](#2Sam.20.25)) and Solomon ([1 Kings 4:4](#1Kgs.4.4)). He is first mentioned as coming to take part with David at Hebron ([1 Chr. 12:27](#1Chr.12.27), [28](#1Chr.12.28)). He was probably on this account made ruler over the Aaronites (27:17). Zadok and Abiathar acted as high priests on several important occasions ([1 Chr. 15:11](#1Chr.15.11); [2 Sam. 15:24-29](#2Sam.15.24), [35](#2Sam.15.35), [36](#2Sam.15.36)); but when Adonijah endeavoured to secure the throne, Abiathar went with him, and therefore Solomon “thrust him out from being high priest,” and Zadok, remaining faithful to David, became high priest alone ([1 Kings 2:27](#1Kgs.2.27), [35](#1Kgs.2.35); [1 Chr. 29:22](#1Chr.29.22)). In him the line of Phinehas resumed the dignity, and held it till the fall of Jerusalem. He was succeeded in his sacred office by his son Azariah ([1 Kings 4:2](#1Kgs.4.2); comp. [1 Chr. 6:3-9](#1Chr.6.3)).
The father of Jerusha, who was wife of King Uzziah, and mother of King Jotham ([2 Kings 15:33](#2Kgs.15.33); [2 Chr. 27:1](#2Chr.27.1)).
The sons of Baana, one of those who assisted in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem ([Neh. 3:4](#Neh.3.4)).
“The scribe” set over the treasuries of the temple by Nehemiah along with a priest and a Levite ([Neh. 13:13](#Neh.13.13)).
One of the two kings of Midian whom the “Lord delivered” into the hands of Gideon. He was slain afterwards with Zebah ([Judg. 8:5-21](#Judg.8.5)).
Id., one whose descendants returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel ([Ezra 2:8](#Ezra.2.8); [Neh. 7:13](#Neh.7.13)); probably the same as Zatthu.
Terror, one of the “dukes of Edom” ([Gen. 36:27](#Gen.36.27)); called also Zavan ([1 Chr. 1:42](#1Chr.1.42)).
Plenty, a descendant of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:33](#1Chr.2.33)).
A Korhite porter of the Lord’s house ([1 Chr. 26:2](#1Chr.26.2)). Three or four others of this name are also mentioned.
A son of Asahel, Joab’s brother ([1 Chr. 27:7](#1Chr.27.7)).
A Levite who took part as one of the teachers in the system of national education instituted by Jehoshaphat ([2 Chr. 17:7](#2Chr.17.7), [8](#2Chr.17.8)).
The son of Ishmael, “the ruler of the house of Judah in all the king’s matters” ([2 Chr. 19:8-11](#2Chr.19.8)).

Man-killer, or sacrifice, one of the two kings who led the vast host of the Midianites who invaded the land of Israel, and over whom Gideon gained a great and decisive victory ([Judg. 8](#Judg.8)). Zebah and Zalmunna had succeeded in escaping across the Jordan with a remnant of the Midianite host, but were overtaken at Karkor, probably in the Hauran, and routed by Gideon. The kings were taken alive and brought back across the Jordan; and confessing that they had personally taken part in the slaughter of Gideon’s brothers, they were put to death (comp. [1 Sam. 12:11](#1Sam.12.11); [Isa. 10:26](#Isa.10.26); [Ps. 83:11](#Ps.83.11)).

A Galilean fisherman, the husband of Salome (q.v.), and the father of James and John, two of our Lord’s disciples ([Matt. 4:21](#Matt.4.21); [27:56](#Matt.27.56); [Mark 15:40](#Mark.15.40)). He seems to have been a man of some position in Capernaum, for he had two boats ([Luke 5:4](#Luke.5.4)) and “hired servants” ([Mark 1:20](#Mark.1.20)) of his own. No mention is made of him after the call of his two sons by Jesus.
Given, the wife of Josiah and mother of Jehoiakim ([2 Kings 23:36](#2Kgs.23.36)).

Habitation, the governor of Shechem under Abimelech ([Judg. 9:28](#Judg.9.28), [30](#Judg.9.30), [36](#Judg.9.36)). He informed his master of the intention of the people of Shechem to transfer their allegiance to the Hivite tribe of Hamor. This led to Abimelech’s destroying the city, when he put its entire population to the sword, and sowed the ruins with salt ([Judg. 9:28-45](#Judg.9.28)).
Dwelling, the sixth and youngest son of Jacob and Leah ([Gen. 30:20](#Gen.30.20)). Little is known of his personal history. He had three sons (46:14).
A Levite who assisted at the bringing up of the ark from the house of Obededom ([1 Chr. 15:20-24](#1Chr.15.20)).

A prophet of Judah, the eleventh of the twelve minor prophets. Like Ezekiel, he was of priestly extraction. He describes himself (1:1) as “the son of Berechiah.” In [Ezra 5:1](#Ezra.5.1) and 6:14 he is called “the son of Iddo,” who was properly his grandfather. His prophetical career began in the second year of Darius (B.C. 520), about sixteen years after the return of the first company from exile. He was contemporary with Haggai ([Ezra 5:1](#Ezra.5.1)).
The father of Abijah, who was the mother of Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 29:1](#2Chr.29.1)).
One of the chiefs of the tribe of Reuben ([1 Chr. 5:7](#1Chr.5.7)).
One who assisted in teaching the law to the people in the time of Jehoshaphat ([2 Chr. 17:7](#2Chr.17.7)).
A Levite of the sons of Asaph ([2 Chr. 20:14](#2Chr.20.14)).
A prophet, who had “understanding in the seeing of God,” in the time of Uzziah, who was much indebted to him for his wise counsel ([2 Chr. 26:5](#2Chr.26.5)).
One of the “rulers of the house of God” ([2 Chr. 35:8](#2Chr.35.8)).

The last king of Judah. He was the third son of Josiah, and his mother’s name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and hence he was the brother of Jehoahaz ([2 Kings 23:31](#2Kgs.23.31); [24:17](#2Kgs.24.17), [18](#2Kgs.24.18)). His original name was Mattaniah; but when Nebuchadnezzar placed him on the throne as the successor to Jehoiachin he changed his name to Zedekiah. The prophet Jeremiah was his counsellor, yet “he did evil in the sight of the Lord” ([2 Kings 24:19](#2Kgs.24.19), [20](#2Kgs.24.20); [Jer. 52:2](#Jer.52.2), [3](#Jer.52.3)). He ascended the throne at the age of twenty-one years. …
The son of Chenaanah, a false prophet in the days of Ahab ([1 Kings 22:11](#1Kgs.22.11), [24](#1Kgs.22.24); [2 Chr. 18:10](#2Chr.18.10), [23](#2Chr.18.23)).
The son of Hananiah, a prince of Judah in the days of Jehoiakim ([Jer. 36:12](#Jer.36.12)).

The wolf, one of the two leaders of the great Midianite host which invaded Israel and was utterly routed by Gideon. The division of that host, which attempted to escape across the Jordan, under Oreb and Zeeb, was overtaken by the Ephraimites, who, in a great battle, completely vanquished them, their leaders being taken and slain ([Judg. 7:25](#Judg.7.25); [Ps. 83:11](#Ps.83.11); [Isa. 10:26](#Isa.10.26)).
Cleft, an Ammonite; one of David’s valiant men ([2 Sam. 23:37](#2Sam.23.37)).

First-born, of the tribe of Manasseh, and of the family of Gilead; died in the wilderness. Having left no sons, his daughters, concerned lest their father’s name should be “done away from among his family,” made an appeal to Moses, who, by divine direction, appointed it as “a statute of judgment” in Israel that daughters should inherit their father’s portion when no sons were left ([Num. 27:1-11](#Num.27.1)). But that the possession of Zelophehad might not pass away in the year of jubilee from the tribe to which he belonged, it was ordained by Moses that his daughters should not marry any one out of their father’s tribe; and this afterwards became a general law ([Num. 36](#Num.36)).

The designation of one of the Phoenician tribes ([Gen. 10:18](#Gen.10.18)) who inhabited the town of Sumra, at the western base of the Lebanon range. In the Amarna tablets (B.C. 1400) Zemar, or Zumur, was one of the most important of the Phoenician cities, but it afterwards almost disappears from history.
Vine-dresser, a Benjamite; one of the sons of Becher ([1 Chr. 7:8](#1Chr.7.8)).
A disciple called “the lawyer,” whom Paul wished Titus to bring with him ([Titus 3:13](#Titus.3.13)). Nothing more is known of him.

The son of Maaseiah, the “second priest” in the reign of Zedekiah, often mentioned in Jeremiah as having been sent from the king to inquire ([Jer. 21:1](#Jer.21.1)) regarding the coming woes which he had denounced, and to entreat the prophet’s intercession that the judgment threatened might be averted ([Jer. 29:25](#Jer.29.25), [26](#Jer.29.26), [29](#Jer.29.29); 37:3; 52:24). He, along with some other captive Jews, was put to death by the king of Babylon “at Riblah in the land of Hamath” ([2 Kings 25:21](#2Kgs.25.21)).
The father of Josiah, the priest who dwelt in Jerusalem when Darius issued the decree that the temple should be rebuilt ([Zech. 6:10](#Zech.6.10)).
A son of Tamar ([Gen. 38:30](#Gen.38.30)); called also Zara ([Matt. 1:3](#Matt.1.3)).
One of the sons of Simeon ([Gen. 46:10](#Gen.46.10); [Ex. 6:15](#Exod.6.15)).

An “Ethiopian,” probably Osorkon II., the successor of Shishak on the throne of Egypt. With an enormous army, the largest we read of in Scripture, he invaded the kingdom of Judah in the days of Asa ([2 Chr. 14:9-15](#2Chr.14.9)). He reached Zephathah, and there encountered the army of Asa. This is the only instance “in all the annals of Judah of a victorious encounter in the field with a first-class heathen power in full force.” The Egyptian host was utterly routed, and the Hebrews gathered “exceeding much spoil.” Three hundred years elapsed before another Egyptian army, that of Necho (B.C. 609), came up against Jerusalem.
Star of Venus, the wife of Haman, whom she instigated to prepare a gallows for Mordecai ([Esther 5:10](#Esth.5.10)).
Stricken, mother of Jeroboam, the first king of the ten tribes ([1 Kings 11:26](#1Kgs.11.26)).

The seed of Babylon, the son of Salathiel or Shealtiel ([Hag. 1:1](#Hag.1.1); Zorobabel, [Matt. 1:12](#Matt.1.12)); called also the son of Pedaiah ([1 Chr. 3:17-19](#1Chr.3.17)), i.e., according to a frequent usage of the word “son;” the grandson or the nephew of Salathiel. He is also known by the Persian name of Sheshbazzar ([Ezra 1:8](#Ezra.1.8), [11](#Ezra.1.11)). In the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, he led the first band of Jews, numbering 42,360 ([Ezra 2:64](#Ezra.2.64)), exclusive of a large number of servants, who returned from captivity at the close of the seventy years. …

Stricken of the Lord, David’s sister, and the mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel ([1 Chr. 2:16](#1Chr.2.16)), who were the three leading heroes of David’s army, and being his nephews, they were admitted to the closest companionship with him.

Post; statue, “a servant of the house of Saul” ([2 Sam. 9:2](#2Sam.9.2)), who informed David that Mephibosheth, a son of Jonathan, was alive. He afterwards dealt treacherously toward Mephibosheth, whom he slanderously misrepresented to David.
The mother of King Joash ([2 Kings 12:1](#2Kgs.12.1); [2 Chr. 24:1](#2Chr.24.1)).
A Levite, one of the sons of Asaph ([Neh. 11:17](#Neh.11.17)); probably the same as Zichri ([1 Chr. 9:15](#1Chr.9.15)), and Zaccur ([Neh. 12:35](#Neh.12.35)).
Another of the same tribe ([1 Chr. 8:23](#1Chr.8.23)).
The Lord is righteous, one who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah ([Neh. 10:1](#Neh.10.1)).

A fishery, a town on the Mediterranean coast, about 25 miles north of Tyre. It received its name from the “first-born” of Canaan, the grandson of Noah ([Gen. 10:15](#Gen.10.15), [19](#Gen.10.19)). It was the first home of the Phoenicians on the coast of Palestine, and from its extensive commercial relations became a “great” city ([Josh. 11:8](#Josh.11.8); [19:28](#Josh.19.28)). It was the mother city of Tyre. …
The name of a family of Nethinim ([Ezra 2:43](#Ezra.2.43); [Neh. 7:46](#Neh.7.46)).
Shadow, one of the wives of Lamech, of the line of Cain, and mother of Tubal-cain ([Gen. 4:19](#Gen.4.19), [22](#Gen.4.22)).
Drooping, Leah’s handmaid, and the mother of Gad and Asher ([Gen. 30:9-13](#Gen.30.9)).
One of the captains of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:20](#1Chr.12.20)).
Vine-dressers; celebrated, one of the sons of Abraham by Keturah ([Gen. 25:2](#Gen.25.2)).

Murdered Elah at Tirzah, and succeeded him on the throne of Israel ([1 Kings 16:8-10](#1Kgs.16.8)). He reigned only seven days, for Omri, whom the army elected as king, laid siege to Tirzah, whereupon Zimri set fire to the palace and perished amid its ruins (11-20). Omri succeeded to the throne only after four years of fierce war with Tibni, another claimant to the throne.
A little bird, the father of Balak, king of Moab ([Num. 22:2](#Num.22.2), [4](#Num.22.4)).

A female bird. Reuel’s daughter, who became the wife of Moses ([Ex. 2:21](#Exod.2.21)). In consequence of the event recorded in [Ex. 4:24-26](#Exod.4.24), she and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, when so far on the way with Moses toward Egypt, were sent back by him to her own kinsfolk, the Midianites, with whom they sojourned till Moses afterwards joined them (18:2-6).
The Lord protects, a Levite, son of Uzziel ([Ex. 6:22](#Exod.6.22)).
The father of Ephron the Hittite ([Gen. 23:8](#Gen.23.8)).
Snatching (?), one of the sons of Ishi ([1 Chr. 4:20](#1Chr.4.20)).
Spreading out, a son of Helem ([1 Chr. 7:35](#1Chr.7.35)), a chief of Asher.

Chirping, one of Job’s friends who came to condole with him in his distress ([Job 2:11](#Job.2.11). The LXX. render here “king of the Mineans” = Ma’in, Maonites, [Judg. 10:12](#Judg.10.12), in Southern Arabia). He is called a Naamathite, or an inhabitant of some unknown place called Naamah.
Honeycomb, a Kohathite Levite, ancestor of Elkanah and Samuel ([1 Sam. 1:1](#1Sam.1.1)); called also Zophai ([1 Chr. 6:26](#1Chr.6.26)).
One of the five Midianite kings whom the Israelites defeated and put to death ([Num. 31:8](#Num.31.8)).
Rock of God, chief of the family of the Merarites ([Num. 3:35](#Num.3.35)) at the time of the Exodus.
Rock of the Almighty, the father of Shelumiel, who was chief of the tribe of Simeon when Israel was encamped at Sinai ([Num. 1:6](#Num.1.6); [2:12](#Num.2.12)).

Heb. ‘Anakim ([Deut. 2:10](#Deut.2.10), [11](#Deut.2.11), [21](#Deut.2.21); [Josh. 11:21](#Josh.11.21), [22](#Josh.11.22); 14:12, 15; called “sons of Anak,” [Num. 13:33](#Num.13.33); “children of Anak,” 13:22; [Josh. 15:14](#Josh.15.14)), a nomad race of giants descended from Arba ([Josh. 14:15](#Josh.14.15)), the father of Anak, that dwelt in the south of Palestine near Hebron ([Gen. 23:2](#Gen.23.2); [Josh. 15:13](#Josh.15.13)). They were a Cushite tribe of the same race as the Philistines and the Egyptian shepherd kings. David on several occasions encountered them ([2 Sam. 21:15-22](#2Sam.21.15)). From this race sprung Goliath ([1 Sam. 17:4](#1Sam.17.4)).
